overview: Attiwonderonk, often called the Neutral, were Iroquoian-speaking communities of southwestern Ontario. Their best-documented confederacy belongs to the seventeenth century, later than this map’s 1492 to 1500 interval. Earlier village archaeology illuminates their regional background; the broad outline should not be read as a surveyed border of one unchanged state.

periods.title: Earlier village communities
periods.summary: Farming villages such as Norton and Lawson reveal the region’s earlier settlement history.

periods.title: The historic confederacy
periods.summary: Political leadership, trade and warfare connected communities in the Hamilton and Niagara region.

periods.title: Dispersal and inherited histories
periods.summary: War broke apart the confederacy, while survivors joined other Iroquoian communities.

items.text: The name Neutral referred to a position between the Huron-Wendat and the Haudenosaunee. It did not mean that these communities never fought. The name describes one set of relationships in a changing political world, rather than a permanent rule of peaceful behavior.

Archaeologist William Noble interpreted early seventeenth-century society under Tsouharissen as a chiefdom, drawing on settlement patterns, trade, historical accounts and oral tradition. His argument emphasizes unusually concentrated leadership linking several communities. It remains an interpretation of political organization, rather than a surviving written constitution.

A pipeline survey in 1988 uncovered Norton village in present-day London, Ontario. Researchers identified nine longhouses, pottery, clay pipes, deer antler and charred corn. The excavation report places occupation around 1400 to 1450; the local library describes its connection with the later Attawandaron as probable.

Lawson occupied a plateau above the meeting of Medway River and Snake Creek. Its longhouses, defensive works and rubbish deposits preserve a substantial farming village of the 1500s. The national designation associates it with ancestral Neutral communities; the museum uses the broader description of an ancestral Indigenous village.

At Lawson, people lived in the village year-round while farming corn, beans and squash and making seasonal trips to hunt, fish and gather. A permanent home therefore belonged within a much wider working landscape. Fields, streams and forests each supplied different parts of the household’s needs.

Objects at Lawson indicate connections reaching Lake Superior, the Atlantic coast and regions south of the Great Lakes. Such finds trace exchange networks beyond the village’s own fields and streams. A small object in a household could have a surprisingly long travel history.

During excavation in 1982, a large pot emerged in pieces from a pit beneath a longhouse bench. Its fragments had been deliberately arranged around the pit’s bottom and edges. Someone had given a broken vessel another job, rather than simply scattering the pieces outside.

Researchers fitted enough of those fragments together to rebuild almost two-thirds of the vessel. Its rim had raised points but no decoration. Digital reconstruction now lets the museum explore missing shapes while limiting handling of the originals. It is a demanding jigsaw puzzle whose pieces cannot be replaced.

Hood, near Freelton, preserves a later Neutral village dated around 1640. Paul Lennox’s 1977 investigation examined longhouses, a palisade and large rubbish deposits. Animal bones, pottery and stone-working debris let researchers study meals, containers and toolmaking alongside the village’s layout.

The Hood collections also contain metal ornaments, jewelry and useful implements acquired through contact and exchange. Imported materials entered a setting where people still made pottery and stone tools. Household belongings accumulated through several kinds of skill and connection at once.

sections.title: A recorded name and a lasting heritage

items.text: A small written trace is “Ounontisaston,” a town name recorded in a 1627 letter. Linguist Charles Julian suggests “Mountain Corner” as a possible meaning. The translation is tentative: only a few possible Neutral names survive, so this is a historical transcription, not a securely translated everyday sentence.

Around 1650, warfare combined with disease and hunger to break apart the confederacy. Survivors became part of other Iroquoian communities. A political name disappearing from reports does not mean that every family died; people continued their lives under changed circumstances and affiliations.

At Lawson, archaeological excavation stopped in 2011. The museum shifted attention toward conservation and stewardship, acknowledging that earlier research often excluded Indigenous participants. Caring for the surviving site now matters as much as finding another object beneath it.

ending.text: The confederacy was dispersed in the wars of the early 1650s, long after the imported 1500 cutoff. Survivors joined other communities; their histories cannot be reduced to a claim that an entire people vanished.
